THOUGHT: This 4-year-old girl presents with a classic triad of systemic symptoms suggestive of hematologic malignancy: (1) constitutional symptoms (prolonged fatigue, fever), (2) signs of bone marrow failure (anemia → pallor and fatigue; thrombocytopenia → easy bruising and low platelet count of 27,000/mm³), and (3) extramedullary disease manifestations (hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy). The severe nocturnal leg pain is highly concerning for bone pain due to marrow expansion from leukemic infiltration — a red flag in pediatrics. The CBC shows marked leukocytosis (63,000/mm³) with concurrent anemia and thrombocytopenia — a “leukemia gap” (i.e., elevated WBC but low RBCs and platelets), which is typical of acute leukemia rather than reactive processes like infection or inflammation. While infectious causes (e.g., EBV, CMV, sepsis) can cause fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly, they rarely cause isolated profound thrombocytopenia with bone pain and marrow replacement. The bone marrow aspirate showing predominance of immature cells immunophenotypically positive for CD10, CD19, and TdT is diagnostic: CD10 and CD19 are B-lymphoid lineage markers, and TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase) is expressed in immature lymphoid precursors — together, this profile is pathognomonic for B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (formerly B-ALL). Age (peak incidence 2–5 years), clinical presentation, lab findings, and immunophenotype all converge on acute lymphoblastic leukemia, B-lymphoblastic type.

DIAGNOSIS: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
